thread.title: AI At The Edge: Nvidia's Robotics Opportunity - NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) | Seeking Alpha

author: Mark Hibben
title: AI At The Edge: Nvidia's Robotics Opportunity - NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) | Seeking Alpha
text:
Rethink Technology business briefs for June 12, 2018.
The potential of AI at the edge
Source: Loup Ventures .
Artificial Intelligence (AI) at the Edge entails building machine intelligence into low power, usually mobile processors that can be used in everything from smartphones to personal robots. To some degree, interest in AI at the Edge is driven by simple capability. It has become possible to build substantial machine intelligence into processors like Nvidia's ( NVDA ) Xavier ARM system on chip (SOC), which powers the latest version of its Drive system for autonomous vehicles.
The potential of endowing virtually every Internet of Things device with machine intelligence has prompted some observers to tout Edge AI as a huge opportunity. Last year Tom Bittman of Gartner wrote a seminal blog The Edge Will Eat The Cloud in which he discussed the advantages of Edge AI:
The agility of cloud computing is great – but it simply isn’t enough. Massive centralization, economies of scale, self-service and full automation get us most of the way there – but it doesn’t overcome physics – the weight of data, the speed of light. As people need to interact with their digitally-assisted realities in real-time, waiting on a data center miles (or many miles) away isn’t going to work. Latency matters. I’m here, right now, and I’m gone in seconds. Put up the right appealing advertising before I look away, point out the store that I’ve been looking for as I drive, let me know that a colleague is heading my way, help my self-driving car avoid other cars through a busy intersection. And do it now.
Latency is one of the key issues that will drive Edge AI, but it's not the only one. Apple ( AAPL ) has fastened on user security and privacy as key drivers for its own Edge AI efforts, that I'll describe in more detail in a companion article.
Dan Woods, writing in Forbes , believes that the Edge AI opportunity is at least as great as the cloud:
. . . there is good reason to believe that there will be more need for AI at the edge than in the cloud. Most of the infrastructure that runs the world today does so using simple rules, without any intelligence. Making all of that infrastructure smarter is going to require a massive amount of understanding of many different contexts. . . at the edge there will be hundreds of players because there is such diversity of infrastructure, data, and application needs.
It's an interesting argument that the variety of infrastructure contexts will drive Edge AI, but I'm not convinced that the presumed adaptability of Edge AI will overcome the economies of scale resident in the cloud. In general, I expect cloud AI to dominate except where issues such as latency or security become paramount.
One of the areas where latency has become a dominant factor is in self-driving cars. Controlling a moving vehicle, making split-second decisions in response to changes in the driving environment, all require on-board intelligence.
Much of that on-board intelligence amounts to advanced motor skills: the ability to control the movement of a robot without damaging the environment or the robot, or injuring people. But even motor skills akin to what people have are fairly challenging for robots, and they're an area where the latency of our communications infrastructure is unacceptable.
The self-driving car can be considered as just one example of a large emerging class of “collaborative robots”. Unlike the industrial robots used for repetitive assembly tasks, collaborative robots can be (by definition) safely used around people, and have the ability to interact with people with some degree of intelligence.
Collaborative robots represent one of the key opportunities for Edge AI. In addition to requisite motor skills, collaborative robots have to be endowed with a suite of sensors that enable the robot to navigate its environment and safely interact with people. As in the example of the self-driving car, the sensor suite can be quite extensive, generating a massive amount of data that would be impractical to transport in real time to a cloud-based system.
Thus, the need to process vast amounts of sensor data, often in the form of high definition video imagery, also mandates resident AI capability in the collaborative robotic device.
Nvidia announces Jetson Xavier at Computex
This year at Computex, Nvidia announced the Jetson Xavier computer. For several years, Nvidia has marketed compact, single board computers powered by its Tegra ARM based SOCs for robotics applications. The centerpiece of Jetson Xavier is the Xavier processor that is also at the heart of Nvidia's Drive Xavier system for autonomous vehicle (NYSE: AV ) applications.
Announced in September 2016, Xavier has figured prominently in Nvidia's marketing of its AV Drive processors and accompanying software. Xavier was launched at CES this year during a presentation by CEO Jensen Huang.
Nvidia claims that Xavier is the most complex SOC ever made, and it certainly is the most complex ARM SOC ever made. In comparison to its 9 billion transistors and 350 mm^2 area, the Apple A11 Bionic has only 4.3 billion transistors and 90 mm^2 area. Xavier is capable of a total of 30 TOPS (trillion operations per second) of mixed precision deep learning with a power consumption of just 30 Watts.
Xavier only started sampling at the beginning of the year, but as production has ramped up, Nvidia was motivated to find other applications for it, and Jetson was a natural fit.
As befits a processor designed for collaborative, intelligent robots, Jetson Xavier has a wealth of I/O including inputs for up to 16 simultaneous cameras, USB 3.1, gigabit Ethernet, and HDMI 2.0. Jetson Xavier is also endowed with perhaps the most powerful GPU of any low power SOC, with 512 Volta architecture cores. Machine learning tasks are accelerated by Volta Tensor Cores along with a pair of deep learning accelerators. Jetson Xavier is also remarkably compact with dimensions of 100 x 87 x 16 mm (not including connectors or heat sink).
Nvidia Jetson Xavier external package. Source: Nvidia .
An important advantage for Nvidia's products has been the software Nvidia has developed for machine learning and GPU computing. Nvidia provides a comprehensive suite a machine learning and image processing tools for its Drive AV systems.
For Jetson, Nvidia has crafted a set of robotics software tools dubbed Isaac. As described in Nvidia's announcement, Isaac consists of:
Isaac SDK– a collection of APIs and tools to develop robotics algorithm software and runtime framework with fully accelerated libraries.
Isaac IMX–Isaac Intelligent Machine Acceleration applications, a collection of NVIDIA-developed robotics algorithm software.
Isaac Sim– a highly realistic virtual simulation environment for developers to train autonomous machines and perform hardware-in-the-loop testing with Jetson Xavier.
Through Nvidia's work in AVs, it's become clear that the ability to train robotic AIs in simulation is essential. Nvidia offers a similar capability for its Drive software.
The combination of powerful hardware and software makes Jetson Xavier one of the most compelling platforms for robotics development available. There simply is no other company in the world that offers a robotics processing platform with the capabilities of Jetson Xavier.
The collaborative robot opportunity
Jetson has been little more than a sideline for Nvidia, especially when previous generations were powered by Nvidia's not particularly distinguished Tegra SOCs. I think that changes very dramatically with the advent of Xavier.
What's the opportunity for collaborative robots? As of Nvidia's latest Investor Day presentation , the interest in collaborative robots was represented by AVs, robotaxis, and trucks. But there is good reason to believe that the opportunity in other types of collaborative robots is quite large.
Gene Munster's Loup Ventures (LV) has published as series of reports giving its outlook for the growth of collaborative robots (excluding autonomous vehicles). For industrial robots, LV foresees much faster growth than in traditional industrial robots.
Within the Commercial Robotics category, autonomous guided vehicles (for logistics applications, excludes robo-taxis and AVs), drones, and medical robots all require extensive sensor suites and machine vision capabilities, combined with on-board machine intelligence. LV sees Commercial Robotics in general as a higher growth area than Industrial, and these are mostly collaborative applications:
LV estimates the total market opportunity for Industrial Collaborative Robots and Commercial Robots to be about $29 billion in five years. The cost of processors and associated software will probably take a significant fraction of that. I would guess that fraction to be at least 20% or $5.8 billion. This number, more than half of Nvidia's fiscal 2018 revenue, is the approximate TAM by 2023.
This may not seem like a huge amount of growth, but investors should keep in mind that Jetson rides on top of the AV development effort. Nvidia gets Jetson's revenue for a modest incremental investment, since the processor will be identical to the Drive system, and the software requires relatively modest additional effort.
In its 2018 Investor Day presentation, Nvidia estimated its TAM for robo-taxis (autonomous ride sharing services) to be about $20 billion, while the larger self-driving car TAM was estimated to be $40 billion, all by 2035.
It's not clear how quickly AV technology will be deployed by the auto industry (thus the 2035 target date), but probably robo-taxis will appear first. They're already being deployed on a trial basis. Probably robo-taxis will achieve mass deployment by some time around 2023.
That makes the total collaborative robotics TAM about $26 billion for Nvidia by 2023, and I expect Nvidia to capture most of that opportunity. Combined with Nvidia's $50 billion datacenter TAM, I expect Nvidia to at least triple its revenue and earnings within five years. Nvidia is by no means overvalued. I remain long Nvidia.
Nvidia is part of the Rethink Technology portfolio and is rated a buy.
